blindSummary:
This state/province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in the country: the national human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to a UN human-rights treaty body documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by this state/province's own police - or by third parties under police cover - against trans and trans-feminine people during operations in three of its cities, including its seat of government, carried out under "preventive policing" frameworks. Academic legal analysis (a national human-rights organisation's shadow report to a UN women's-rights treaty body, plus university legal commentary) confirms that after the 2012 national gender-identity law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased their use of drug-law prosecution (devolved to this state/province's own courts in 2005) and of street-offence codes as the operative instrument for indirect criminalisation of trans and trans-feminine identity - a patterned, state-implicated escalation with impunity.

The position is modestly below the national average. No other state/province has a comparable volume of multi-source, patterned enforcement documentation reaching the UN treaty-body system. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework (drug-law devolution plus anti-narcotics security policy) that measurably increased police persecution of trans women. Protective institutions coexist - the state/province's own rights-ombudsman office maintains a 2024 registry-rectification guide and documents discrimination caseloads - but these are resident-facing and do not offset the visitor-facing exposure to arbitrary detention during any police stop.

Compared with the autonomous capital city, this state/province lacks the capital's dedicated contravention-court oversight structure and anti-discrimination apparatus; its offence-code court model gives less post-detention review. Compared with the silent majority of state/provinces, the difference is one of documented pattern rather than statutory hostility - no law of this state/province criminalises gender identity, but enforcement practice does the work.
